newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Kras to target new markets, boost range.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Kras to target new markets, boost range.

text.p: Croatia's leading confectionery manufacturer Kras plans to expand in eastern and central European markets, including former Yugoslavia, and increase its products range, a company official said on Friday.

"Our next long-term step will be to focus on Polish market...and on markets that emerged after the breakup of Yugoslavia, once political problems are solved," assistant export manager Darko Radisic told Reuters by telephone.
"Our products are very well known on (former Yugoslav) markets and we would be very eager to regain our place there," he said.

Kras is Croatia's largest chocolate-maker with a 40.5-percent market share, with annual output of some 22,000 tonnes of chocolate, wafers and other sweet products. Its 1996 net profit rose to 18.56 million kuna.
"Kras increases its market share in Croatia every year. For this autumn we plan several new products for the home market," Radisic said. "Of course, we also want to freshen up our offer abroad."

Earlier this month the company said it hoped to raise 60 million marks from foreign lenders to finance its development plans and has mandated Germany's Bayerische Vereinsbank to arrange the syndication, due to be completed by September.

The company recently adopted a new business strategy until the year 2000, with plans to spend some 51 million German marks to modernise its outdated production lines and open new production facilities.
Bayerische will immediately grant Kras a bridging loan of 20 million marks so it can repay old debts and place orders for new equipment. Another 10 million marks will be made available by year-end.
The company plans to draw on the other 30 million mark tranche some time next year, but officials said it might still opt out if it finds "cheaper funds through equity investment."

Kras also intends to boost its equity by 271.5 million kuna or 50 percent. It has been negotiating for the past year with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) but a deal has remained elusive so far.
The company sells 51 percent of its output domestically and exports the rest to its neighbours and other countries worldwide.
Radisic said the company hoped to focus on countries
belonging to Central European Free Trade Association (CEFTA), once Croatia joins the organisation.

The company is already more than 50 percent privatised, with current and former employees controlling around 25 percent of its stock and other private investors 20.65 percent. It also has 11.41 percent in treasury shares.
The rest is split between the state privatisation agency, which will put its shares into a mass voucher scheme later this year, and two state pension funds.
Kras's shares have been recently trading around 400 kuna on the Zagreb Stock Exchange. The stock closed at 410 kuna on Friday, ater opening at 400 on Tuesday.
